name: Musée National du Burkina Faso
overview: State museum on a 29-hectare site in Ouagadougou, facing the Charles de Gaulle paediatric hospital, at the end of Boulevard Thomas Sankara (Wikipedia).

Created in 1962 and long a project. The foundation stone was laid on 23 October 2000 and the museum was inaugurated on 23 December 2004. It became a state public institution of a scientific, cultural and technical character (EPSCT) on 20 March 2002 (Wikipedia).

Mission: to collect and conserve the material and immaterial witnesses of the country's ethnocultural communities and to teach Burkinabè people about their heritage (Director General Sabari Christian Dao, Lefaso.net, 3 November 2024).
funding_verdict: Musée National du Burkina Faso: public: a state museum, with local government and company donations for its 2026 renovation drive

name: Bandjoun Station
overview: Artist-run contemporary art centre, museum, residency and farm in Bandjoun, western Cameroon, in the Bamileke highlands (Africultures, The Art Newspaper's French edition).

Founded by the artist Barthélémy Toguo, who describes it as a "laboratoire sans frontières" (Africultures, translation). Toguo is artistic director, Germain Noubi managing director and Carine Djuidje handles cultural mediation (Contemporary And).

Opening date: sources differ. Africultures (Erika Nimis, 17 February 2015) says Toguo started it in 2000 and it officially opened in November 2013. Apollo (20 March 2025) says Toguo launched it in 2007. The Art Newspaper's French edition (23 September 2019) says it opened to the public in 2013 and was officially inaugurated on 16 November 2016 after eight years of construction, with the then minister Ama Tutu Muna attending. Contemporary And gives 2013 in its text and 2007 in its background notes.
funding_verdict: Bandjoun Station: self-funded: the founder's own money, with coffee sales and a friends' association

press_items.title: Fleur Macdonald, "'Bandjoun Station is an imposing proposition'" (20 March 2025)
Esther Poppe, "Bandjoun Art Station: The Importance of a Peripheral Institution in Cameroon" (27 February 2020)
Monique Ngo Mayag, "Bandjoun Station, cinq ans d'engagements tous azimuts" (23 September 2019)

name: doual'art
overview: Contemporary art centre and experimental laboratory for new urban practices in African cities, at Place du Gouvernement in Douala (stated by the space).
Founded in 1991 by Marilyn Douala Bell and Didier Schaub, and registered as a non-profit in 1992. Douala Bell is president, and Schaub was artistic director until his death in 2014 (Wikipedia).
Its exhibition space, Espace doual'art, opened in 1995 in Bonanjo, in the former cinema of the Palace of Douala Kings, a building owned by the Douala Bell family (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: doual'art: grant-funded: international foundations and agencies

name: Musée National du Cameroun
overview: National museum of Cameroon in Yaoundé, housed in the former presidential palace (museum website).
President Paul Biya assigned the site to the museum on 17 November 1988 (museum website).

The building covers 5,000 m² with about 30 rooms. Le360 reports it reopened on 16 January 2014 after about five years of closure for rehabilitation, while AFD dates the reopening to 2015 (Le360, 30 July 2019; AFD).
funding_verdict: Musée National du Cameroun: public: a French debt-conversion grant for its modernisation, with the Cameroonian Ministry of Arts and Culture as counterpart

name: Dalhousie Art Gallery
overview: University art gallery at 6101 University Avenue, Halifax, in the Dalhousie Arts Centre of Dalhousie University (stated by the gallery; Canadian Encyclopedia).

Began in October 1953 as one room in the Arts and Administration Building, run by faculty volunteers, growing out of an informal university art group. It moved to the Dalhousie Arts Centre in November 1971 (Dal News, Kevin Bradley, 3 December 2014). The Canadian Encyclopedia calls it the oldest public art gallery in Halifax and says it has had full-time professional staff since 1972.
Building: the Dalhousie Arts Centre is in a pseudo-brutalist style of raw concrete walls, and replaced a row of Edwardian houses (Dal News, 2014).
funding_verdict: Dalhousie Art Gallery: university gallery with public grants: Dalhousie University, Canada Council for the Arts, Canadian Heritage

name: Musée d'art de Joliette
overview: Art museum in Joliette, Quebec, in front of the Outaragawe sipi (L'Assomption River). Its architecture is inspired by the international style and the ideas of Le Corbusier (museum website).

Origins in 1943, when Father Wilfrid Corbeil of the Clercs de Saint-Viateur set up a painting gallery at the Séminaire de Joliette. In 1966 the Clercs entrusted the collection to a committee. The museum moved to the former Scolasticat Saint-Charles in 1969. Construction of the present building began on 26 August 1974 and it opened to the public on 25 January 1976 (museum website, history page).
Collection of about 8,300 works in four areas: Canadian art, European art, contemporary art and archaeology (museum website).
funding_verdict: Musée d'art de Joliette: non-profit supported by Quebec and Canadian public bodies, its own foundation and corporate and family partners

name: Galerie de l'UQAM
overview: University contemporary art gallery in the Pavillon Judith-Jasmin, room J-R120, 1400 rue Berri, Montréal (stated by the gallery).
Part of the Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM). French Wikipedia dates the gallery to 1975 and its move to the Pavillon Judith-Jasmin to 1979.
French Wikipedia lists Louise Déry as director.
funding_verdict: Galerie de l'UQAM: mainly public: a university gallery with the Canada Council for the Arts and the Conseil des arts et des lettres du Québec (CALQ) as named partners

name: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec
overview: Quebec's national fine arts museum, in Battlefields Park, Quebec City: a complex of four buildings connected by tunnels (Wikipedia).

A fine-arts collection was created in 1920. The Musée de la Province was inaugurated in 1933, became the Musée du Québec in 1963, a state corporation under the Loi sur les musées nationaux in 1984, and took its present name in 2002 (museum website).

Buildings (Wikipedia): the Gérard-Morisset Pavilion by Wilfrid Lacroix (built 1928 to 1931), the Charles Baillairgé Pavilion (a prison of 1867 renovated in 1989 to 1991), the Grand Hall visitor centre, and the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion by the Office for Metropolitan Architecture, opened in June 2016 at a cost of about C$103.4 million. Construction of the Espace Riopelle began in spring 2024 (museum website).
funding_verdict: Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec: state corporation of the Government of Quebec, with corporate sponsors and donors

name: Owens Art Gallery
overview: University art gallery at 61 York Street, Sackville, New Brunswick, part of Mount Allison University (Owens Art Gallery website).

Opened on 28 May 1895 to house the collection of the Owens Art Institution, which had been established in Saint John, New Brunswick, in 1884. About 400 paintings and 100 plaster casts moved to Sackville (Mount Allison library guide). CTV News (Alana Pickrell, 17 May 2025) calls it the oldest university art gallery in Canada.

Designed by Edmund Burke in the Beaux-Arts style, with a light olive sandstone facade, stone and brick, and terra-cotta friezes on three sides. The 1972 renovation by Gustavo Da Roza & Brown, Brisley & Brown added an expanded entryway at the rear and replaced the atrium skylights with upstairs gallery space (Mount Allison library guide).
funding_verdict: Owens Art Gallery: mainly public: Canada Council for the Arts, the New Brunswick government and Mount Allison University

name: Winnipeg Art Gallery-Qaumajuq
overview: Public art gallery in downtown Winnipeg: the 1971 main building and Qaumajuq, a building for Inuit art opened in March 2021 (Wikipedia; The Art Newspaper).
Its roots go back to the Winnipeg Museum of Fine Arts, opened on 16 December 1912; the present Winnipeg Art Gallery was incorporated by the Manitoba legislature on 6 May 1963 (Wikipedia).
Qaumajuq is Inuktitut for "it is bright, it is lit" (The Art Newspaper).
funding_verdict: Winnipeg Art Gallery-Qaumajuq: mixed public and private: governments and private donors built Qaumajuq, and Nunavut pays to keep its collection there

press_items.title: Gabriella Angeleti, "World's biggest Inuit art collection revealed at Winnipeg's new museum within a museum" (2021)
Elena Goukassian, "Canadian museum removing name of former director and Nazi supporter Ferdinand Eckhardt from its entrance hall" (2024)

name: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Santiago
overview: Contemporary art museum of the University of Chile, run through the university's Faculty of Arts, with two sites: Parque Forestal and Quinta Normal (Diario Financiero, 31 July 2021; University of Chile news, 17 May 2021).
Operating since 1947 (Francisco Brugnoli, El Mostrador, 22 December 2014).
Both sites together cover more than 5,000 m², with 32 staff in 2021 (Diario Financiero, 31 July 2021).
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Santiago: public: the University of Chile

name: Guangdong Times Museum
overview: Non-profit contemporary art museum at Times Rose Garden Phase III, Huangbian North Road, Baiyun District, Guangzhou. The exhibition hall is on the 19th floor of a residential tower, open 10:00 to 18:00 (Baiyun District government page, 25 May 2022; ArtAsiaPacific).

Set up in 2003 as a branch of the Guangdong Museum of Art, co-founded by Times Property (now Times China) and that museum. It became an independent institution and opened to the public on 31 December 2010 (Baiyun District government page).
The exhibition space, 1,200 square metres in ArtAsiaPacific's figure, was designed by Rem Koolhaas and Alain Fouraux (The Art Newspaper, 26 March 2024).
funding_verdict: Guangdong Times Museum: corporate-backed until 2022: developer Times China, now running on a quarter of its budget and seeking several donors

name: How Art Museum
overview: Private contemporary art museum in the Zhangjiang Hi-Tech Park, Shanghai, described as a free-trade zone dedicated to scientific research and development (The Art Newspaper, 22 September 2017, Lisa Movius).

Founded by the hotelier-collector Zheng Hao. It opened on 20 September 2017 as a sister venue to his museum in Wenzhou, which opened in 2013. An earlier plan to open in Waigaoqiao was cancelled in 2014 (The Art Newspaper).
The name is HOW Art Museum.
funding_verdict: HOW Art Museum: self-funded: the private wealth of founder Zheng Hao, described as a hotelier and a real estate figure
wider_context: The Art Newspaper (Lisa Movius, 27 September 2023) reported that many Chinese private museums depend on parent companies to pay their bills, and named the collapsing property market and tightening censorship among the pressures behind closures and downsizings.
The same article lists HOW Art Museum among the boom-era private museums "plodding away through these lean years", not as closed or downsized.

press_items.title: Pamela Wong, "Artist Demands Compensation from Shanghai Private Museum for Unreturned Artworks" (5 November 2020)
Richard Whiddington, "How The New HOW Art Museum Is Beating All Expectations With A New Museum Model" (2019)

name: Hubei Museum of Art
overview: Provincial art museum at No. 1 Sanguandian, Donghu Road, Wuchang District, Wuhan, on the East Lake shore next to the Hubei Provincial Museum (Hubei Department of Culture and Tourism; China Daily).
It is managed by the Hubei Department of Culture and Tourism, which describes it as a government-invested public-interest cultural institution (Hubei Department of Culture and Tourism, in Chinese).

It opened on 6 November 2007 and became free to enter on 30 October 2008. It was renamed from 湖北省艺术馆 to 湖北美术馆 in July 2010 and was named a first-batch National Key Art Museum by the Ministry of Culture in 2011 (Hubei Department of Culture and Tourism, in Chinese).
funding_verdict: Hubei Museum of Art: mainly public: provincial government

name: Museo La Tertulia
overview: Modern and contemporary art museum on the bank of the Cali River at El Charco del Burro, in the west of Cali (Wikipedia, El País).

Founded on 9 March 1956 in a house in the San Antonio neighbourhood rented by the journalist Alfonso Bonilla Aragón (Wikipedia). El País (Rosa Isabel Pelaez, 9 March 2023) credits a group of Cali cultural figures led by Maritza Uribe Urdinola. Wikipedia says Clara Inés Suárez and Maritza Uribe de Urdinola set up the cultural group. It began as a free school for 50 low-income pupils and a café bar with talks, exhibitions and film at night (El País). Earlier name: Museo de Arte Moderno La Tertulia, changed in 2016 (El País).
A "tertulia" is a social gathering, especially to talk about art or literature (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo La Tertulia: partners named by the museum are Colegio Alemán de Cali, Bancolombia, Fundación Sura, Comfandi and Fundación Scarpetta Gnecco; Ministry of Culture project calls

name: Museo de Antioquia
overview: Art museum at Carrera 52 No. 52-43 in Medellín (museum website).

Began in 1872 as the Museo de Zea, founded by Manuel Uribe Ángel, Antonio José Restrepo and Martín Gómez. In 1946 a group including Teresa Santamaría and Joaquín Jaramillo Sierra reopened it as a private non-profit entity. It received legal status from the Gobernación in 1953 (Spanish Wikipedia). The English page and Minuto30 give 1881 as the founding year.

Since 2000 it occupies the former Palacio Municipal, an Art Deco building won in a 1931 council competition by H. M. Rodríguez e Hijos and built from 1932 to 1937. It housed the city government until 1988, when it passed to Empresas Públicas de Medellín. It was declared a national monument in 1995 (Spanish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo de Antioquia: mixed: a private non-profit financed by public programmes and corporate allies

name: Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (MAMM)
overview: Modern and contemporary art museum at Carrera 44 N° 19A-100 in Ciudad del Río, Medellín.

Founded in 1978 and opened on 17 November 1978 by a group of artists of the "generación urbana", with architects and businesspeople. It followed the interest generated by the Coltejer Art Biennials of 1968, 1970 and 1972 (Spanish Wikipedia).
In 2009 the Medellín city government assigned it the Talleres Robledo building, a steelworks dating from 1938 in the Ciudad del Río industrial zone. An expansion opened in 2015 (Spanish Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín: mixed: own earnings, corporate and foundation sponsors, and city and national public money
wider_context: El Espectador (Redacción Economía and Redacción Política, "Lo que viene tras fallo de responsabilidad fiscal por Hidroituango", 6 September 2021) reported that Colombia's Contraloría General de la República found 26 of 28 people and entities fiscally responsible, for gross negligence ("culpa grave"), in the Hidroituango dam project. The damage ruled on is 4.3 billones of pesos (4.3 trillion), in a first-instance decision open to appeal. The responsible parties named include Sergio Fajardo, Alonso Salazar, Luis Alfredo Ramos and the CCC Ituango consortium companies (Camargo Correa, Conconcreto and Coninsa Ramón H.). EPM is the company developing the project and is not named among those found responsible.

The article does not mention MAMM. The connection is that EPM, the company developing the project, is listed as a pillar sponsor on the museum's sponsors page and supported Cine MAMM in 2023 (2023 management report).

name: Museo de Arte Costarricense (MAC)
overview: National art museum in the La Sabana area of San José, in the former terminal of La Sabana airport (Wikipedia).
Created by Law No. 6091 of 7 October 1977. Inés Trejos Araya led its founding, and it opened on 5 May 1978 (Juan Carlos Flores Zuñiga, Meer, 10 October 2023).
The airport was built in 1937 and closed in 1974, the terminal was named architectural heritage in 1986, and it was renovated and reopened in October 2011 on a site of about 10,800 m² (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte Costarricense: public: Costa Rica's Ministry of Culture and Youth

press_items.title: Juan Carlos Flores Zuñiga, "A 45 años del Museo de Arte Costarricense" (10 October 2023)

name: Museo de Arte y Diseño Contemporáneo
overview: State contemporary art and design museum on Avenida 3, calle 15, San José, inside the Centro Nacional de la Cultura (Cenac), which belongs to the Ministerio de Cultura y Juventud (La Nación; Wikipedia).

Opened on 21 February 1994 in the former Fábrica Nacional de Licores (Fanal), and the collection began with 196 works under the direction of Virginia Pérez-Ratton (La Nación, Fiorella Resenterra and Daniel Soto Morúa, 27 July 2019).
Law 7758 of 1998 created the museum as a body of "maximum deconcentration" of the Ministry of Culture, with its seat at the Cenac (text of the law on the museum's site).
funding_verdict: Museo de Arte y Diseño Contemporáneo: mainly public: Costa Rica's Ministry of Culture through the national budget
wider_context: Semanario Universidad (Natalia Díaz Zeledón, "Artistas y trabajadores de cultura marchan por San José contra recortes presupuestarios", 24 October 2020) reported that artists and arts workers marched in San José against budget cuts negotiated in the Legislative Assembly: about 4,100 million colones approved by the Comisión de Hacendarias, affecting several institutions under the Ministry of Culture and Youth. Photographer and visual artist Sara Mata said her collective began organising over news of a merger of the Museo de Arte Costarricense and the MADC, and that the merger was part of the government's proposal to the International Monetary Fund.
The MADC is one of the two museums named in the proposed merger, it is an agency of that ministry, and the article's photo caption places a protest near the MADC.

name: Galerie Rudolfinum
overview: Contemporary art gallery at Alšovo nábřeží 12, Prague 1, in a neo-Renaissance building on the bank of the Vltava that it shares with the Czech Philharmonic (stated by the gallery).
Founded in 1994 (gallery website). Wikipedia gives the opening as 1 January 1994 and says it has no permanent collection and about 1,500 square metres of exhibition space.
The Rudolfinum building was designed by Josef Zítek with Josef Schulz, opened on 8 February 1885 and is named for Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Galerie Rudolfinum: public institution supported by the Czech Ministry of Culture, with private patrons, a technology partner and earned income
